section.title: The Bride's Nighttime Search
section.sectionRationale: After the joy of the garden comes a night of missed connection and painful longing. The bride hears her beloved knocking but hesitates to open; when at last she rises, he has gone. She searches the city, is beaten by the watchmen, and can only plead with the daughters of Jerusalem to tell him she is sick with love. It is the Song’s most honest picture of love strained by hesitation and absence.
section.thesis: Love is tested by hesitation and absence: the bride delays to open to her knocking beloved, finds him gone, seeks him through a hard night, and, wounded but undeterred, pleads that he be told she is faint with love.
section.frameNote: Two movements: the knock and the missed opening, the beloved calling in the night and the bride’s costly hesitation; and the painful search, the watchmen’s blows, and her plea, tell him I am sick with love.

units.label: The knock and the missed opening
units.note: I opened, but he had gone

verses.text: I sleep, but my heart is awake. A sound! My {{dodi|beloved}} is knocking: “Open to me, my sister, my darling, my dove, my flawless one. My head is drenched with dew, my hair with the dampness of the night.”
I have taken off my robe; must I put it back on? I have washed my feet; must I soil them again?
My {{dodi|beloved}} put his hand to the latch; my heart pounded for him.
I rose up to open for my beloved. My hands dripped with myrrh, my fingers with flowing myrrh on the handles of the bolt.
I opened for my beloved, but he had turned and gone. My heart sank at his departure. I sought him but did not find him. I called, but he did not answer.

units.label: The painful search and the plea

verses.text: I encountered the watchmen on their rounds of the city. They beat me and bruised me; they took away my cloak, those guardians of the walls.
O daughters of Jerusalem, I adjure you, if you find my beloved, tell him I am sick with {{ahavah|love}}.

dodi.gloss: Beloved, the bride’s characteristic name for her man, my beloved, dodi. Here he is the one knocking in the night and then, painfully, the one she seeks after her hesitation.

ahavah.gloss: Love. The bride is holat ahavah, sick or faint with love, undone by longing for her absent beloved; love here is shown as costly and consuming, not merely pleasant.

basic.context: After the joy of the garden comes a hard night. The bride is half asleep when her beloved knocks and asks her to open. She hesitates, making small excuses, and by the time she rises and opens, he has gone. Her heart sinks. She searches the city, and this time the watchmen beat her and take her cloak. All she can do is beg the other women: if you find him, tell him I am sick with love.
basic.hermeneutics: This is the most painful scene in the Song, and it is deeply honest. On the plain level it shows how hesitation and self concern can wound even a real love, and how longing can become an ache that costs something to pursue. Within the whole Bible, it also pictures the soul that grows slow toward God, feels His seeming absence, and must seek Him again with renewed longing. The scene warns and it comforts.
basic.originalLanguages: Her man is again dodi, my beloved, who knocks and calls her his flawless one even as she delays. When she is undone by his absence she calls herself sick with love, holat ahavah, faint with longing. The same word ahavah that filled the garden with delight now aches with absence.
basic.typology: The beloved who comes knocking and is left waiting pictures the Lord who stands at the door and knocks, and the sorrow of the delayed opening warns against a heart grown slow toward Him. The renewed, costly search pictures repentance and the recovery of first love.
basic.christ: Behold, I stand at the door and knock, says the risen Christ to a lukewarm church. The bride’s hesitation is a mirror of every heart that grows comfortable and slow to answer Him, and her aching search is the way back, longing for His presence again. Christ does not despise the one who seeks Him with tears.
basic.god: God draws near and seeks fellowship with His people, and He feels, as it were, the grief of being met with delay. Yet He is not finally lost to those who seek Him; the very ache He allows can rekindle a love grown cold.
basic.crossReferences: Revelation 3:20, I stand at the door and knock. Revelation 2:4 to 5, you have abandoned your first love; return. Psalm 30:5, weeping may stay for the night, but joy comes in the morning.
basic.oneStory: This night of missed connection sings honestly of love strained by hesitation and absence. It warns against a heart grown slow toward the One who knocks, and it points to the renewed, longing search that finds Him again, the recovery of first love in Christ.

context.literary:
This short scene is a deliberate mirror of the first night search in 3:1-5, and the reader is meant to hold the two side by side. In chapter 3 the bride lies on her bed seeking the one she loves, rises to go about the city, meets the watchmen, passes them and finds him almost at once. Here the roles reverse. He seeks her, she is slow, he has gone, she searches, she meets the watchmen and this time they strike her, and no finding is reported. The same words, 'I sought him but did not find him', are repeated from 3:1-2 and now end with a silence.

The scene is also built as a short drama in three beats. Verses 2 to 4 describe the knock and her hesitation in the present tense of memory, with the hand at the latch as the hinge. Verses 5 and 6 turn on a single verb, 'I opened', and the discovery that he has already gone. Verses 7 and 8 take the search into the street and end with a charge to the daughters of Jerusalem.

The poem begins with a puzzling line, 'I sleep, but my heart is awake'. It tells the reader that the story is told from a border between sleep and waking, and may be a dream, or may be a night remembered with a dreamlike blur. The scene ends not with a resolution but with a request, and the answer is delayed until the friends' question in 5:9, which opens the next poem. The reader is left with the weight of her longing in the way the bride is left with it.
context.historical:
The setting is a house at night in a walled city. A beloved at the door in the dark was not strange: courtship and married life took place in a world where a man might come to the door of the family house by night. The door was secured by a bolt, and the handles of verse 5 belong to that kind of fastening. The beloved's head is wet with the dew and the drops of the night, which suggests that he has been waiting outside for some time.

The daughters of Jerusalem and the watchmen belong to the city. The watchmen walked the streets and the walls, as in Isaiah 62:6 where the Lord sets watchmen on the walls of Jerusalem, and their task was to keep order. A woman alone in the street at night might arouse suspicion, and the watchmen's treatment of her here as a suspect is harsh but not unthinkable, which is why the text calls them 'guardians of the walls' with some irony. In 3:3 the same watchmen simply met her. The change shows how a dark night can bring a different outcome.

The cloak that is taken is a garment that offered protection and some dignity. The Torah protects a poor man's cloak, forbidding a creditor to keep it overnight, Exodus 22:26-27, so the loss of a cloak is a real hardship and a real shame. Perfumed oil on a woman's hands as she goes to open the door is a sign of preparation, a bride who had anointed herself for her husband, and here perhaps a sign that her heart had turned toward him even before she moved.
context.canonical:
The scene stands in the long biblical tradition of the seeker who is not found at once. The Psalms are full of it: 'My soul thirsts for God, the living God. When shall I come and appear in God's presence?' Psalm 42:2. The Lord invites it, 'Seek the LORD while He may be found; call on Him while He is near,' Isaiah 55:6, and promises, 'You will seek Me and find Me when you search for Me with all your heart,' Jeremiah 29:13. In Hosea 5:15 He Himself withdraws until His people 'seek My face', and in their affliction 'they will earnestly seek Me'.

The knock at the door is taken up directly by the risen Christ in Revelation 3:20, 'Behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone hears My voice and opens the door, I will come in and dine with him, and he with Me.' In the same letter He says 'Those I love, I rebuke and discipline,' 3:19, and in the letter to Ephesus He says 'you have abandoned your first love,' 2:4. Jesus also tells His disciples to be like servants who open at once when their master comes and knocks, Luke 12:36.

The night search finds an echo on the morning of the resurrection. Mary Magdalene goes to the tomb while it is still dark, John 20:1, and when Jesus asks her, 'Whom are you seeking?' she is still searching, 20:15, until He speaks her name. The disciples on the road to Emmaus tell a similar story: He seems to go farther and they press Him to stay, Luke 24:28-29, and then their eyes are opened. In each of these the one who seeks finds that the beloved has been drawing near all along.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The poet means to tell the truth about love, and part of that truth is that it can fail in small ways. The first hearers would know that even in a marriage that is real and warm, there are nights when comfort wins over closeness. She is not unfaithful, and she is not uncaring, yet she lets a minor inconvenience, a robe and washed feet, hold her back from a loving request. The poet puts this in the book on purpose, because a picture of love that had no shadows would not be believed.

The scene also teaches what to do with such a failure. Her heart pounds when she hears him at the latch, and she rises at once. She does not stay in bed to nurse her guilt. She goes out, she searches, she accepts risk and humiliation, and she asks for help. The poem presents repentance as costly pursuit, with no excuses left.

Finally, the poet wants hearers to see that love has stakes. The beloved went away, and the heart sinks. A reader who thinks that love can be treated as a convenience is told that closeness can be lost for a night and must sometimes be recovered with pain. At the same time the scene is unfinished and hopeful, because the next poem shows her speaking of him with confidence.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
This is a narrative of one night and nothing in it is a command. It does not say that a wife must open at once to her husband, and it does not teach that watchmen may beat a woman for being out at night. The beating is part of what happens, not what ought to happen, and the text calls the watchmen 'guardians of the walls' in a way that exposes their failure.

What the passage does teach by description is that love sometimes involves delay and distance, that the delay is felt, and that the response is to go and seek. The reader should resist two misuses. One is a use that shames those in marriage who experience difficult nights, as if the passage proved that every cold moment was the wife's fault. The other is a spiritual use that makes every dry period in a believer's life the sign of a lapse. The text allows both to be true: sometimes the delay is our own, and sometimes the absence is only a stretch of longing.

What carries over with confidence is that closeness is worth pursuing, that comfort is a poor reason to keep a door shut, and that love is worth a price. Those lessons apply to marriage, friendship and prayer alike.

debates.question: What kind of book is the Song: a celebration of married love, an allegory of Christ and the church, or both?

views.label: A celebration of covenant married love
views.case: The scene reads naturally as a real strain within marriage, hesitation, missed connection, and the ache of separation, honest about love’s hard nights as well as its joys, Proverbs 5 and Genesis 2.

views.label: An allegory of Christ and the church, or God and Israel
views.case: The church has heard here the soul grown slow toward the Lord who knocks, and the seeming absence that follows spiritual coldness, in step with Revelation 3:20 and the call to recover first love.

views.label: Both, the literal strain as a God-given sign
views.case: The fullest reading keeps both: the poem honestly voices a hard night of married love, and because that love is a God-given sign, Ephesians 5:31 to 32, the delayed opening and painful search rightly picture the soul’s coldness toward Christ and the renewed longing that seeks Him again.

debates.bearing: Holding both keeps the passage honest about love’s trials while letting it search the heart: it neither pretends love is always easy nor loses the warning against growing slow toward the One who knocks.

debates.question: Is the scene a dream, or an event that happened?

views.label: A dream or night vision
views.case: The opening line, 'I sleep, but my heart is awake,' places her between sleep and waking. The sudden shifts, the vanishing of the beloved and the odd encounter with the watchmen all suit a dream, and the first night search in 3:1 also begins on her bed.

views.label: A real event, told as memory
views.case: The verbs are narrative and the details are concrete: the latch, the myrrh on the bolt, the watchmen, the loss of the cloak. Nothing in the text says 'I dreamed', and the poem may simply be a woman recalling a real night.

views.label: A poetic scene with no need to decide
views.case: Love poetry is not required to separate memory from imagination. The scene may be a stylized picture of an emotional truth, and its function is the same whether or not it was dreamed.

debates.bearing: Because the text never settles the question, the lesson does not depend on the answer. The scene is true to the experience of love lost and sought, and the lack of explanation invites the reader to enter it.

debates.question: Was her hesitation a fault, or only a mild reluctance?

views.label: A real failure of love
views.case: She was asked to open and offered excuses about a robe and her feet. The immediate sorrow when he leaves, and her grief, suggest that she regarded it as a lapse. The pattern of Revelation 3:20 supports hearing in it the warning of a heart slow to respond.

views.label: Playfulness or modesty
views.case: Some hear teasing in her words: a night-time banter between lovers, with the delay a game that went further than meant. On this reading nothing is amiss with her love, and only the timing went wrong.

views.label: An ordinary human weakness
views.case: The text does not use a word for sin or blame. It describes tiredness and comfort, a normal weakness, and invites the reader to feel its cost without condemning her.

debates.bearing: The text records the delay without a verdict and lets the consequence speak. Whatever her motive, the passage teaches that love can be strained by small hesitations and that the right response is to rise and seek.

study.originalLanguages:
The scene opens with a paradox: 'I sleep, but my heart is awake.' The verb for sleep is the ordinary root, the one Psalm 121:4 denies of the Protector of Israel, who 'will neither slumber nor sleep', and the word for awake carries the sense of being alert. The paired lines describe a body at rest and a heart on watch, which is already the language of longing.

The beloved speaks in four endearments, 'my sister, my darling, my dove, my flawless one.' The last is a word that means whole or complete, from the family of the word used of Job as blameless, so he addresses her as whole and unspoiled even while she hesitates. Her answer in verse 3 is two questions, 'must I put it back on?', and the verbs are strikingly physical: she has stripped off her robe and washed her feet. The excuses are small, concrete and a little comic.

In verse 4 the text says that he put his hand to the latch, but the Hebrew word is more like a hole or opening, and translations differ about whether it was a latch-hole in the door. Then 'my heart pounded' is literally a word for the inward parts, which stirred or moaned for him. The same noun and verb are used in Jeremiah 31:20 of the Lord, whose inward being yearns for Ephraim, and the BSB there reads 'My heart yearns for him.' The longing in the Song is therefore described in a physical depth that Scripture elsewhere applies to God.

In verse 5 her hands drip with 'flowing myrrh', a phrase that has to do with liquid myrrh that passes or runs, so that the very bolt she touches is wet with perfume. The excuses have just been given, and now her hands are scented for him.

Verse 6 holds a notable difficulty. The BSB reads 'My heart sank at his departure.' The Hebrew is literally 'my soul went out when he spoke', and the sense is debated: it may mean that she nearly fainted at his word, or that her life went out of her at his leaving. The translation chooses the second.

The last verse carries a formula from earlier in the Song. 'I adjure you' is the oath she used in 2:7 and 3:5 to charge the daughters not to stir up love until it pleases. Now the oath is turned to a different purpose, a request to tell him she is faint with love, using the same phrase as 2:5.

typology.fulfillment: The beloved stands outside, wet from the night, and asks to be let in. Christ says the same: 'Behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone hears My voice and opens the door, I will come in and dine with him, and he with Me,' Revelation 3:20. In Luke 12:36 He tells His servants to open at once when their master knocks. The type shows the Lord as a visitor who respects the door. It falls short because the beloved in the Song is bound by the night and by the hour, while Christ's knock is the patient mercy of One who holds all time.

The bride's excuses mirror a heart grown comfortable. Christ tells the church at Ephesus that she has abandoned her first love and calls her to repent and do her first deeds, Revelation 2:4-5, and the same warning appears in the parable of the ten virgins, who were not ready when the bridegroom came, Matthew 25:1-10. The correspondence is the cost of a missed opportunity. The type falls short because Revelation also promises forgiveness to those who repent, while the closed door in Matthew 25 is a final warning.

The bride searches the city, is struck, and loses her cloak, yet keeps seeking. This is the pattern of the faithful in distress: 'in their affliction they will earnestly seek Me,' Hosea 5:15, and 'You will seek Me and find Me when you search for Me with all your heart,' Jeremiah 29:13. Mary Magdalene seeks in the dark, John 20:1, and is asked 'Whom are you seeking?' before she hears her name, John 20:15-16. The type falls short because the bride must search, whereas the Lord has already gone before His people.

The bride ends the night asking for help and calling herself faint with love. The Psalms offer the promise that 'weeping may stay the night, but joy comes in the morning,' Psalm 30:5, and the disciples on the Emmaus road find that their hearts burned when the risen Lord spoke, Luke 24:32. The type falls short because the Song leaves the night unresolved in this poem, whereas the gospel brings the morning of the resurrection.

study.christ:
The passage leads to Christ most directly by the knock. In Revelation 3:20 the risen Lord speaks to a church that has grown lukewarm, and He speaks in the language of the Song: He stands at a door, He knocks, He asks to be let in, and He promises fellowship at table. The bridegroom in the Song who has waited in the night is a fitting picture of this Christ, whose patience is greater than our comfort. The image is not meant to suggest that He needs us, but that He chooses to wait for us.

The Gospel of John gives the pattern a second shape. Mary Magdalene goes to the tomb in the dark, John 20:1, finds it empty and weeps. She says 'They have taken the Lord out of the tomb, and we do not know where they have put Him,' 20:2. Jesus asks her 'Woman, why are you weeping? Whom are you seeking?' 20:15. She is looking for the beloved and cannot see him standing next to her, and then He says her name, 'Mary,' and she knows Him. The bride's night in the city is not the same as Mary's morning, but both tell of longing that has not yet found.

The scene also touches Christ through His own suffering. The bride is struck and stripped by the guardians of the city, a small and inverted echo of the One who was struck and stripped by those who should have guarded justice, Matthew 27:28-31. The echo should not be pressed as allegory. What the passage does allow is a pattern of love that pays a price for the sake of the beloved, and it is Christ who pays it fully.

Finally, the poem leads to Christ by what it leaves unresolved. The ache of the bride is real and unfinished. The church lives in that interval: she has the Bridegroom's promise and she awaits His coming, and so she says in the last words of Scripture, 'Come, Lord Jesus.' Jesus Himself says, 'the bridegroom will be taken from them; then they will fast,' Matthew 9:15, and the longing of the Song is the holy longing of that time. The reunion is promised in Revelation 19:7 and 21:2, and until then the church seeks, calls and does not give up.
study.god:
The passage shows a God who comes to His people and does not hold back from asking. The knock at the door is His initiative. In the Song the beloved approaches, speaks tenderly, and addresses her by names of love even when she is slow. Revelation 3:19 says 'Those I love, I rebuke and discipline,' and the same Lord stands at the door. He is the God who 'longed to gather' the children of Jerusalem 'but you were unwilling,' Matthew 23:37, and the Song's missed opening gives a human face to that grief.

It shows God as a feeling God. The Song's word for what stirs in the bride's depths is the word used in Jeremiah 31:20 for the yearning of the Lord Himself, 'My heart yearns for him,' says God of Ephraim. This does not make God subject to the passions of a creature, but it does show that Scripture speaks of His love as something that moves Him, and that the longing of a lover is a true if limited picture of it.

The passage holds together two things that can seem to pull apart: God's nearness and His apparent absence. The beloved is at the door and then gone. Hosea 5:15 says that the Lord withdraws until His people seek His face, and Isaiah 55:6 calls us to seek Him while He may be found. These texts do not mean that He is fickle, but that He uses absence to draw out love. A heart that has grown used to His presence can be roused by missing it.

The scene also shows God's mercy toward the seeker. The bride is wounded, and yet she is not condemned. The Lord promises 'You will seek Me and find Me when you search for Me with all your heart,' Jeremiah 29:13, and Deuteronomy 4:29 says the same.

For worship this means a double posture. We listen for the knock and open without delay, and when we have been slow we do not hide but go out to seek. We also pray with the honesty of the Psalms, 'My soul longs, even faints, for the courts of the LORD,' Psalm 84:2, and the church is allowed to say, as the bride says, that she is sick with love.

crossReferences.note: The first night search, which this scene mirrors. There she seeks, meets the watchmen, passes them, finds him and holds him. In 5:2-8 the watchmen strike her and she does not find him. Reading them together shows how love can move from quick joy to slow ache.

'Sustain me with raisins; refresh me with apples, for I am faint with love.' The words she repeats in 5:8 first appear here. In chapter 2 the faintness is delight, while in chapter 5 it is the pain of absence, and the same phrase carries both.

Christ stands at the door and knocks, and promises to come in and dine with the one who opens. It is the clearest New Testament use of the Song's knocking beloved, addressed to a church whose love has grown cool.

The Lord charges Ephesus with abandoning her first love and calls her to remember, repent and do the first deeds. It describes the spiritual condition behind the bride's hesitation, and the path back.
Servants are to open to their master at once when he comes and knocks. The verse gives the standard against which the bride's delay is measured, a ready heart that responds promptly to the knock.
Ten virgins wait for the bridegroom, and some are unprepared when he comes at midnight. The parable shares the Song's night-time arrival and the danger of being found unready.

The Lord says of Ephraim, 'My heart yearns for him.' The word for yearning is the same one used of the bride's inward stirring in Song 5:4, so the Song's ache of love is echoed in the Lord's own longing.

The Lord returns to His place until His people seek His face, and in their affliction they will earnestly seek Him. It supplies the theology of absence behind the Song's search: sorrow that is meant to turn the heart.

'You will seek Me and find Me when you search for Me with all your heart.' It offers the promise that the Song's unfinished search is not in vain, since the one who seeks with the whole heart will find.
Mary weeps at the tomb and does not recognise Jesus until He says her name. Her night of seeking and the Lord's question 'Whom are you seeking?' bring the Song's search to its New Testament morning.
'Weeping may stay the night, but joy comes in the morning.' The psalm offers the comfort that the Song leaves for later: a night of sorrow is not the last word.

study.oneStory:
The night search belongs to a story in which God knocks and humanity is slow to answer. In creation God walks in the garden looking for His people, and the first couple are silent and hide, Genesis 3:8-9. The pattern is set early: the Lord calls and the creature delays. Throughout the Old Testament He sends prophets who rise early and speak, and Israel is slow to respond, and He says through Hosea that He will withdraw until they seek His face, Hosea 5:15.

The Song places that pattern inside a marriage, and in doing so makes it intimate. The beloved is not a distant judge but a lover at the latch, and the failure is not a rebellion but a small hesitation. Even so, the pain of the night is real. Love can be lost for a time and recovered only by seeking, and the poem refuses to hide the cost.

Redemption comes as the Lord who knocks becomes the Lord who comes. In Christ, God does not wait outside the door only; He enters the world, is struck by the guardians of the city, loses His cloak, and goes through the night for His people, Matthew 27:28-31. He says to a cool church, 'Behold, I stand at the door and knock,' Revelation 3:20, and on the first morning He stands beside a weeping woman and says her name, John 20:15-16. The longing of the Song finds its answer in the One who is both the seeker and the sought.

The story ends in a place where there is no more night. Revelation 21:25 says that the gates of the new city will never be shut, and the bride who once searched the streets by night is brought home as 'a bride adorned for her husband,' Revelation 21:2. The bolt on the door and the watchmen on the walls belong to the world of the fall. In the new creation there is no door to open, because the Beloved is among His people, and the church's lasting prayer, 'Come,' is answered. Until then, the church can learn from the bride: to listen, to rise, to seek, and to trust that the longing is itself a gift.

quiz.q: What happens when the beloved knocks in 5:2 to 6?

options.text: The bride hesitates with small excuses, and by the time she opens, he has gone.
options.note: Her delay costs her the meeting; he has turned and left.

options.text: She opens at once and welcomes him in gladly.
options.note: She hesitates first, and the delay is the heart of the scene.

options.text: She refuses to acknowledge that he is there.
options.note: She does hold back and fail to open in time, but she hears him and her heart pounds; she delays rather than flatly refusing to acknowledge him.

options.text: He forces the door open against her will.
options.note: He does put his hand to the latch, but he then withdraws and departs; he does not force the door against her will.

quiz.q: What do the watchmen do this time, in 5:7?

options.text: They beat and bruise her and take away her cloak.
options.note: The search now turns costly and dangerous.

options.text: They kindly help her find her beloved.
options.note: In the earlier night search the watchmen were harmless, but this time, unlike then, they wound her rather than help.
They do fail to help her, but they go further than ignoring her; they beat her and take away her cloak.

options.text: They bring her beloved to her.
options.note: She does not find him here; she can only plead with the daughters of Jerusalem.

quiz.q: What does the bride mean when she says she is sick with love?

options.text: She is faint and undone with longing for her absent beloved.
options.note: Love here is costly and consuming, aching in his absence.

options.text: She has lost all feeling for him.
options.note: The reverse: she is overwhelmed by longing for him.
Her love does bring her real pain, but she does not regret it; she aches to be with him and pleads that he be told.

options.text: She is physically ill from the night air.
options.note: The language is truly of faintness and bodily weakness, but the cause is love-longing for her absent beloved, not merely the night air.

quiz.q: How does the knocking beloved point to Christ?

options.text: He echoes the risen Christ who stands at the door and knocks, calling a lukewarm church to open to Him.
options.note: The scene warns against growing slow toward the One who draws near, Revelation 3:20.

options.text: He teaches that Christ gives up on those who hesitate.
options.note: He does withdraw when she delays, but he does not give up; the way back is a renewed search, and Christ calls the lukewarm to return.

options.text: He shows that seeking Christ again is pointless.
options.note: The aching search is the path to recovering first love.

options.text: He has no connection to Christ at all.
options.note: The scene truly tells of human lovers, yet Scripture ties the knocking beloved to the risen Christ at the door, Revelation 3:20, so it points beyond itself.

questions: The bride hesitated over small comforts and missed her beloved. Where have small excuses made you slow to answer God when He drew near?
Behold, I stand at the door and knock. Is there a way Christ has been knocking in your life that you have been slow to open to?
Her search became costly, and still she pressed on. What would it look like to keep seeking the Lord even when it is hard and you feel wounded?
She was undone, sick with love, in her beloved’s absence. Have you known a longing for God’s nearness that ached when He felt distant, and how did you seek Him?
The scene points to the recovery of first love. If your love for Christ has cooled, what one step might you take this week to seek Him again with renewed longing?

translationNotes.note: I sleep, but my heart is awake sets the dreamlike, half waking tone of the scene.
My heart sank at his departure renders a phrase for the soul going out or failing, the ache of loss at his absence.
Sick with love, holat ahavah, means faint or overwhelmed with longing, as also at 2:5.

meta.notes: BSB text fetched from bible.helloao.org for Song of Solomon 5:2-8, chapter 5. Poetic lines rendered as flowing prose within each verse.
